days.title: ATP Computation Practice
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compute ATP yields for respiration stages.
  • Compute ATP needs for photosynthesis.
  • Interpret ATP yield problems.
  • Compare photosynthesis and respiration energetics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP yield — total ATP produced.
  • ATP need — total ATP consumed.
  • Efficiency — energy captured vs. total energy.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Respiration ATP Yield

  • Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH
  • Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH
  • Krebs: 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂
  • ETC: 10 NADH × 2.5 + 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 25 + 3 = 28 ATP
  • Total: ~32 ATP

B. Photosynthesis ATP Need

  • Per CO₂: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH
  • Per glucose (6 CO₂): 18 ATP + 12 NADPH

C. Efficiency Comparison

  • Respiration captures ~34% of glucose energy as ATP.
  • Photosynthesis captures ~1% of solar energy.

💬 Let's Discuss

This week you will use what you know to solve problems. ATP computations look hard, but they all use a few conversion factors, just like converting pesos to dollars. Memorize this short list:

  • Aerobic respiration: about 32 ATP per glucose (2 glycolysis + 2 Krebs + ~28 ETC).
  • ETC: ~2.5 ATP per NADH, ~1.5 ATP per FADH₂.
  • Fermentation: 2 ATP per glucose.
  • Calvin cycle: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂, so 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.

Step 1: identify the process (respiration, fermentation or Calvin cycle). Step 2: find the rate per unit (per glucose, per CO₂ or per carrier). Step 3: multiply, and check the units.

Example 1: How much ATP comes from 5 glucose fully oxidized? 5 × 32 = 160 ATP. Example 2: How much ATP is needed to fix 12 CO₂? 12 × 3 = 36 ATP (and that makes 12 ÷ 6 = 2 glucose). Example 3: 10 NADH through the ETC: 10 × 2.5 = 25 ATP. Example 4: 3 glucose fermented: 3 × 2 = 6 ATP — compare with 96 ATP if respired aerobically.

Always read the question carefully. Does it ask for glucose made or broken down? Per CO₂ or per glucose? Modern (32) or older (36–38) values? A small reading error leads to a large answer error.

Common mistake: using the respiration value (32) for a photosynthesis question. Building glucose costs 18 ATP; breaking it down earns about 32.

pairs.why: Glycolysis contributes 2 ATP.
The Krebs cycle contributes 2 ATP per glucose.
The ETC contributes about 28 ATP (25 from NADH + 3 from FADH₂).
2 + 2 + 28 ≈ 32 ATP per glucose.
The Calvin cycle spends 18 ATP to build one glucose.
The Calvin cycle spends 12 NADPH per glucose.

scenarios.text: If 5 glucose are fully oxidized, how many ATP (approx)?
scenarios.explanation: 5 glucose × 32 ATP = 160 ATP.

scenarios.text: How many ATP are needed to fix 12 CO₂?
scenarios.explanation: 12 CO₂ × 3 ATP = 36 ATP.

scenarios.text: If 10 NADH pass through the ETC, ATP produced (approx)?
scenarios.explanation: 10 NADH × 2.5 ATP = 25 ATP.

scenarios.text: How many ATP needed to build 3 glucose?
scenarios.explanation: 3 glucose × 18 ATP = 54 ATP.
2 glucose × 32 ATP = 64 ATP.

scenarios.text: If fermentation occurs, ATP per glucose is:
scenarios.explanation: Fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose.

questions.text: How many ATP are needed to make 2 glucose in the Calvin cycle?
How many ATP does 4 NADH yield in the ETC (modern)?

takeaways: Photosynthesis needs 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.
NADH yields 2.5 ATP; FADH₂ yields 1.5 ATP.
ATP computation is essential for bioenergetics.

days.title: Advantages of Fermentation
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain the advantages of fermentation.
  • Describe situations where fermentation is beneficial.
  • Relate fermentation to real-world applications.
  • Compare fermentation to aerobic respiration.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Fermentation — anaerobic ATP production.
  • Rapid ATP — fast but low yield.
  • Applications — food, industry, medicine.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Advantages of Fermentation

  • Works without oxygen — useful in low-O₂ environments
  • Very fast — quick ATP for short bursts
  • Regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis going
  • Used in food production (bread, cheese, yogurt, beer)
  • Used in biofuel production (ethanol)

B. Where It Happens

  • Muscle cells during intense exercise
  • Yeast in fermentation vats
  • Bacteria in yogurt and cheese

C. Real-Life Examples

  • Sprinting (lactic acid)
  • Bread rising (CO₂ from yeast)
  • Yogurt fermentation (lactic acid bacteria)

💬 Let's Discuss

If aerobic respiration gives about 16 times more ATP, why would any cell ever use fermentation? Because fermentation has real advantages in the right situation.

1. It works without oxygen. Yeast in a sealed jar, bacteria deep in your gut or in a swamp, and muscle cells during a hard sprint can all keep making ATP when oxygen is missing. 2. It is fast. Glycolysis plus fermentation is short and happens right in the cytoplasm, so ATP can be produced very quickly — useful for a 100-meter dash or for lifting something heavy. Sprinters' fast-twitch muscle fibers rely heavily on it. 3. It keeps glycolysis running by regenerating NAD⁺. 4. Its by-products are useful to people.

Humans have used fermentation for thousands of years. Yeast makes pandesal and ensaymada rise with CO₂ and produces ethanol in tuba (coconut wine), basi (sugarcane wine) and in bioethanol fuel from sugarcane. Lactic acid bacteria make yogurt, cheese, burong isda, atchara and kimchi; the acid sours the food and stops spoilage bacteria. Acetic acid bacteria turn alcohol into sukang Iloco and coconut vinegar.

The drawbacks are just as real: only 2 ATP per glucose, so it cannot support long activity, and its products (lactate, ethanol) build up and can become harmful at high levels.

Common mistake: believing lactic acid causes muscle soreness the next day. Lactate is cleared within an hour or so; delayed soreness comes from tiny muscle injuries. Lactate is even recycled by the liver into glucose.

pairs.why: Fermentation produces ATP quickly because it is short and occurs in the cytoplasm.
Fermentation can proceed when oxygen is missing.
Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
CO₂ from yeast fermentation makes bread rise.
Lactic acid bacteria ferment milk into yogurt.
Sprinting muscles produce lactate by fermentation.

scenarios.explanation: Without oxygen, fermentation can still make some ATP.

scenarios.text: Very fast ATP needed for sprinting.
scenarios.explanation: Short bursts like sprinting rely on fast fermentation.
Yeast fermentation makes CO₂ that raises dough.
Lactic acid fermentation by bacteria makes yogurt.
Yeast fermentation produces ethanol for fuel.
Fermentation is faster and does not need O₂, though its yield is low.

questions.text: Which is a key advantage of fermentation?
questions.explanation: The key advantage of fermentation is that it works without oxygen.
Yogurt is made by lactic acid bacteria fermenting milk.

takeaways: It is fast but yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
Widely used in food and industry.

days.title: Advantages of Aerobic Respiration
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain the advantages of aerobic respiration.
  • Compare ATP yield to fermentation.
  • Describe why most organisms use aerobic respiration.
  • Analyze trade-offs between aerobic and anaerobic strategies.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • High ATP yield — 32 ATP per glucose.
  • Complete oxidation — glucose → CO₂ + H₂O.
  • Sustained energy — supports long-term activity.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Advantages of Aerobic Respiration

  • Produces ~32 ATP per glucose (16× fermentation)
  • Sustains long-term activity (endurance exercise)
  • Powers large organisms with high energy needs
  • Allows complex multicellular life

B. Comparison Table

FeatureFermentationAerobic
O₂Not requiredRequired
ATP2~32
SpeedFastSlower
SustainabilityShort burstsLong-term
LocationCytoplasmCytoplasm + mitochondria

💬 Let's Discuss

For anything that lasts more than a couple of minutes, life runs on aerobic respiration. Its main advantage is simple: a far higher ATP yield — about 32 ATP per glucose versus 2 for fermentation. To get the same energy by fermentation, a cell would have to burn through about 16 times more glucose.

Aerobic respiration also gives sustained energy. It can use many fuels — glucose, fats (which yield even more ATP per gram) and, if needed, proteins — and its end products, CO₂ and water, are easy to remove: we breathe out CO₂ and use or excrete the water. Fermentation's products, lactate and ethanol, build up and must be dealt with.

This is why endurance activities depend on oxygen. A marathon runner, a swimmer, or a farmer working in the field all day relies on slow-twitch muscle fibers that are packed with mitochondria, have many capillaries, and are rich in myoglobin (which stores oxygen and makes them red). Training increases the number of mitochondria in muscle cells, so trained athletes can stay aerobic at higher speeds.

The trade-offs are that aerobic respiration requires a steady supply of oxygen, needs mitochondria, and is slower to deliver ATP than fermentation.

Real activity mixes both: a basketball player uses fermentation for quick jumps and sprints, and aerobic respiration for running up and down the court all game. Common mistake: saying aerobic respiration happens only in animals. Plants, fungi and most protists respire aerobically too.

pairs.why: Aerobic respiration yields far more ATP per glucose.
Aerobic respiration can supply energy for long periods.
Long-duration exercise relies on aerobic respiration.
The Krebs cycle and ETC happen in mitochondria.
The modern total is about 32 ATP per glucose.
Aerobic respiration requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

scenarios.explanation: Marathon running depends on sustained aerobic respiration.
A high ATP yield comes from aerobic respiration.
When oxygen is available, cells respire aerobically.
32 ATP per glucose is the aerobic yield.
Long-term, sustainable energy comes from aerobic respiration.
The Krebs cycle and ETC take place in mitochondria.

questions.text: How much ATP does aerobic respiration produce per glucose?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration produces about 32 ATP per glucose.

questions.text: Why can't fermentation sustain long exercise?
questions.explanation: Fermentation gives only 2 ATP per glucose — too little for long activity.
The Krebs cycle and ETC happen in mitochondria.

takeaways: Aerobic respiration produces ~32 ATP per glucose.

days.title: Real-World Applications & Synthesis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Synthesize knowledge of photosynthesis and respiration.
  • Analyze real-world applications.
  • Compare fermentation and aerobic respiration strategies.
  • Evaluate biological trade-offs.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Trade-offs — speed vs. yield.
  • Applications — medicine, industry, sports.
  • Synthesis — energy flow across life.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Real-World Applications

AreaApplication
Food industryFermentation for bread, beer, cheese, yogurt
MedicineCancer cells use aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect)
Sports scienceTraining to increase mitochondria for endurance
BiofuelsEthanol from yeast fermentation
AgriculturePhotosynthesis for crop yield

B. Photosynthesis + Respiration = Life's Energy Cycle

  • Photosynthesis converts light → chemical energy (glucose)
  • Respiration converts chemical energy → ATP
  • Products of one are reactants of the other

C. Key Trade-offs

  • Fermentation: fast but low yield
  • Aerobic: slower but high yield
  • Cells use both depending on conditions

💬 Let's Discuss

Let us put the whole quarter together. Photosynthesis and respiration are two halves of one cycle. Photosynthesis (chloroplasts) uses light, CO₂ and water to make glucose and release O₂. Aerobic respiration (mitochondria) uses glucose and O₂ to make ATP, releasing CO₂ and water. The products of one are the raw materials of the other — the basis of the carbon cycle and the oxygen we breathe.

These processes matter in daily life and the economy. Food production: crop yield depends on how well plants photosynthesize; farmers use enough sunlight, water and fertilizer (magnesium and nitrogen are needed for chlorophyll). Food processing: fermentation gives us bread, cheese, yogurt, vinegar, patis and bagoong. Energy: yeast fermentation of sugarcane and cassava produces bioethanol, blended into gasoline in the Philippines. Health: endurance training increases mitochondria; many cancer cells rely on glycolysis even with oxygen present (the Warburg effect), which doctors use to detect tumors in PET scans. Environment: burning fossil fuels releases ancient carbon faster than photosynthesis can absorb it, raising atmospheric CO₂; forests and mangroves help take it back.

When comparing processes, use four questions: Where does it happen? What goes in? What comes out? How much ATP is made or used? If you can answer these for glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the ETC, fermentation, the light reactions and the Calvin cycle, you have mastered this unit.

Common mistake: saying plants make oxygen "for us." Plants release O₂ as a by-product of splitting water; they use some of it themselves.

pairs.why: Bread, cheese and yogurt are all made by fermentation.
Many cancer cells rely heavily on glycolysis even with oxygen present.
Endurance training increases the number of mitochondria in muscle.
Yeast ferments sugar into ethanol used as fuel.
Crop yield depends on how much sugar photosynthesis produces.
Photosynthesis and respiration cycle carbon between the air and living things.

scenarios.explanation: Splitting water in photosynthesis releases O₂.
Aerobic respiration uses O₂ as the final electron acceptor.
Respiration releases CO₂ from glucose carbons (alcoholic fermentation also releases some).
Photosynthesis fixes CO₂ into sugar.

scenarios.text: Which yields more ATP per glucose?
scenarios.explanation: Aerobic respiration gives about 32 ATP versus 2.
Fermentation is quicker because it is short and happens in the cytoplasm.

questions.text: Which process produces oxygen as a byproduct?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases O₂ by splitting water.

questions.text: Which is the key disadvantage of fermentation?
questions.explanation: Fermentation's main drawback is its low ATP yield.

takeaways: Photosynthesis and respiration form life's energy cycle.
Both pathways are used in different conditions.
Applications span food, medicine, sports, and energy.
